results.content:
The bicycle derailleur is a marvel of mechanical engineering, designed to translate the linear pull of a hand lever into the precise lateral movement of a bicycle chain. To understand how it works, one must look at the synergy between the cable tension, the parallelogram geometry, the jockey wheels, and the chain itself.

### The Cable: The Input of Force
The shifting process begins at the rider's handlebars. When the rider clicks the shift lever, it either releases or increases tension on a steel inner cable. This cable runs along the frame of the bike inside a housing to the rear derailleur. 

When the rider shifts to a larger cog (an "easy" gear), the lever pulls the cable taut. This tension pulls the derailleur inward toward the wheel. Conversely, when shifting to a smaller cog (a "hard" gear), the lever releases tension, allowing a powerful return spring inside the derailleur to pull the mechanism back outward. The cable acts as the primary messenger, initiating the entire mechanical chain reaction.

### The Parallelogram: The Mechanical Pivot
The heart of the derailleur is the parallelogram. This is a frame made of four metal links connected by four pivot points. The primary function of the parallelogram is to ensure that as the derailleur moves laterally (side to side), it remains perfectly perpendicular to the wheel. 

Because of the geometry of the parallelogram, the derailleur arm—the part holding the chain—moves in a straight horizontal line. This is critical because if the derailleur tilted as it moved, the chain would bind or jump unpredictably. By maintaining a vertical orientation, the derailleur ensures that the chain is pushed directly underneath the next sprocket, allowing for a clean transition.

### The Jockey Wheels: Tension and Direction
Attached to the moving arm of the parallelogram are two small pulleys known as jockey wheels: the upper guide and the lower guide. The chain loops around these wheels in a "Z" shape. 

The jockey wheels serve two vital roles. First, they maintain proper chain tension. When the rider shifts to a larger cog, the loop of chain increases; the derailleur's spring pulls the jockey wheels forward to take up the slack, preventing the chain from sagging into the spokes. Second, the upper jockey wheel acts as a guide. As the derailleur moves laterally, the upper jockey wheel pushes against the chain, forcing it to climb the teeth of the next cog.

### The Chain: The Final Output
The chain is the component that actually undergoes the gear change. When the derailleur moves inward, the upper jockey wheel exerts lateral force on the chain. Because the chain is wrapped around the teeth of the sprocket, this force causes the chain links to climb over the teeth of the larger cog. 

Once the chain has gripped the teeth of the new sprocket, the rotation of the pedals pulls the chain across. When shifting downward, the derailleur pulls the chain inward, causing it to drop off the large cog onto the smaller one. This entire process happens in milliseconds, facilitated by the precise tension of the cable, the rigid geometry of the parallelogram, and the constant guidance of the jockey wheels.
